explain.tweet: Everything has an explanation — deny it and you can’t trust your own reasoning. Stones, stars, and universes owe their existence to something else, and no chain of borrowers explains why anything exists. So something exists by its own nature: pure act, one, cause of all. God.
explain.elevator: Everything has an explanation. We assume this in science and in daily life, and if we denied it, we couldn’t trust our own reasoning. Now, most things are explained by something outside them. Their existence is on loan. A chain of borrowers, even an infinite one, never explains why there is any existence to lend. So something must exist by its own nature. And anything like that can’t change or have parts, which rules out the universe. There can be only one such thing. That’s God.
explain.twoMinute:
Here’s the idea. Everything has an explanation — philosophers call this the **principle of sufficient reason**. That doesn’t mean we always *find* the explanation. It means there always *is* one. You already believe this. If your car won’t start, you never think, ‘Maybe it’s failing for no reason at all.’

Could it be false? Think about what that would mean. If things can happen for no reason, then your beliefs could pop into your head for no reason too, including the belief that everything has an explanation, or that it doesn’t. You couldn’t trust your senses or your logic. And science would be hollow: if the deepest laws of physics were brute facts with no explanation, they couldn’t really explain anything built on top of them. That’s like saying a book stays up because it sits on a shelf that floats for no reason.

So accept the principle. Now notice that some things are explained by something *else*. A tree depends on soil, sun, and the laws of physics, and on its atoms holding together right now. Call those things **contingent**. Other things might be explained by their *own nature*. Call those **necessary**.

Could everything be contingent? Suppose an infinite chain, each thing caused by an earlier one. You still haven’t explained why the chain exists, or why it has these laws rather than others, or what keeps this tree existing *this second*. A chain of borrowed existence, however long, is like an infinite line of people borrowing money from each other: nobody ever actually has any money. So something must exist by its own nature.

What would that be like? It couldn’t have unrealized potentials, because then it would depend on whatever realizes them. It couldn’t have parts, because then it would depend on what holds them together. Its very essence would have to be *to exist*. That rules out the universe, which changes and has parts. There can be only one such being, and it’s the cause of everything else. That’s what classical theists have always meant by God.

And God isn’t an exception to the principle. God has an explanation, his own nature. Everything else is explained by him.
explain.eli12:
Imagine you find a cookie on your desk. You’d wonder who put it there, right? You’d never think, ‘It’s just there for no reason.’ That’s the big rule of this chapter: **everything has a reason why it’s there**.

Now, most things are there because of *something else*. The cookie is there because your friend left it. Your friend exists because of her parents. A tree needs sun, soil, and water. Things like that are **borrowers**: they borrow their existence from other things.

Here’s a puzzle. Suppose everybody in a line borrows a dollar from the next person, and the line goes on forever. Does anyone actually get a dollar? No! Somebody has to *have* a dollar that isn’t borrowed. It’s the same with existence. If everything borrowed its existence, there would be no existence to borrow.

So there must be something that doesn’t borrow its existence — something that exists just because of what it is. That thing can’t be made of parts, because parts need to be put together. It can’t change, because changing means depending on something to change you. The universe is made of parts and changes all the time, so it isn’t that thing.

There can only be one thing like that, and everything else gets its existence from it. That’s what people mean by God. And God isn’t cheating the rule. God has a reason for existing too: his reason is just what he is.
whiteboard: Write ‘PSR: Everything has an explanation.’ Beneath it draw two arrows: ‘in something else’ → CONTINGENT, and ‘in its own nature’ → NECESSARY. Cross out a third arrow labeled ‘in nothing’ and say that PSR rules it out.

Box: ‘Why believe PSR?’ List three supports: (1) we always find explanations or know why we can’t; (2) deny it and you can’t trust perception or reasoning — self-undermining; (3) you can’t use explanatory arguments everywhere else and exempt existence without arbitrariness (Della Rocca).
Draw a book on a shelf floating in air with a ‘?’ under the shelf. Write ‘brute-fact law’ on the shelf. Say: if the bottom is unexplained, nothing above it is explained either.

Draw a long chain of circles running off to the left, labeled ‘…C ← B ← A’ with ‘∞’ at the end. Circle the whole chain and write ‘still contingent — why this chain? why these laws?’ Add a little stack of geometry books.
Next to it, draw a pebble and a pile of pebbles. Write ‘weight: ✗ parts→whole; color: ✓ parts→whole; contingency is like color (doubly contingent).’
Draw a second, higher chain above the first labeled ‘contingent cause of the chain’ with an arrow pointing to ‘same problem again → passing the buck.’

Switch to a vertical diagram: a single tree at the bottom, with arrows pointing up to ‘what sustains it NOW?’ → contingent sustainer → contingent sustainer … → NECESSARY BEING at the top. Say: this route needs no claim about the universe as a whole.
Stage 2: write ‘Necessary ⇒ no potentials (pure act), no parts (simple), essence = existence.’ Draw arrows from these back to ‘Ch1 Unmoved Mover, Ch2 the One, Ch4 Subsistent Existence.’
Write ‘Only one possible → cause of everything else → immutable, eternal, immaterial, omnipotent, omniscient, good = GOD.’
Finish with a two-column box: ‘God — self-explanatory (not self-caused)’ vs. ‘Universe — explained by another.’ Say that no exception has been made: everything has an explanation.
explain.keyAnalogy: **Borrowed existence: the endless chain of IOUs.** Ask your listener to imagine needing $100. You borrow it from A, who borrows it from B, who borrows it from C, forever. Does money ever actually arrive? Only if someone in the chain *has* money without borrowing it. Now map it: contingent things have their existence on loan, from their causes and from whatever sustains them right now. Lengthening the chain, even to infinity, only multiplies debts. Adding a second infinite chain of ‘higher’ lenders changes nothing, because they are borrowers too. Only something that *owns* its existence by its very nature can explain why there is any existence to go around. That is a necessary being. Two tips: (1) stress the *here and now*: the loans are being made at this moment, not just in the distant past, so ‘the chain goes back forever’ is no answer; (2) use it to defuse ‘What caused God?’: the rich lender doesn’t need a loan, and that isn’t an exception to how money works but the only way anyone gets paid. Limit: the analogy doesn’t by itself show the necessary being is simple or unique. That takes Stage 2.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes the argument click is that **the demand for explanation is not a theist’s optional extra; it is the price of reasoning at all**, and the argument never exempts God from it. Once someone sees that (a) they rely on PSR every time they trust evidence, infer, or explain anything, and (b) the conclusion is not an unexplained God but a *self-explanatory* one whose nature is existence itself, the ‘special pleading’ charge disappears and the only question left is whether anything else could explain itself.

The argument usually fails to click for two reasons. First, people hear ‘everything has a cause’ instead of ‘everything has an explanation,’ and then ‘What caused God?’ looks devastating. Second, people picture a chain of events stretching back in time to a first moment, so an infinite past seems to defeat the argument. Correct both at the start: explanation, not causation; and dependence *now*, not a starting point in time.

audiences.startingPoint: Science explains everything that can be explained. Explanation bottoms out in the fundamental laws of physics, which just are what they are. Appeals to God look like a ‘god of the gaps.’
audiences.approach: Start *inside* scientific practice. Point out that the whole enterprise assumes there are explanations to find, and that the world’s intelligibility would be a miracle without PSR. Then press the book-and-shelf point: if the fundamental laws are brute, the higher-level explanations physics is proud of are illusory. Present the argument as a question about the *preconditions* of science, not a rival hypothesis. It is not a gap-filler; it asks what makes any law explanatory at all. On quantum mechanics: quantum events are made intelligible by quantum laws, and indeterminism is not unintelligibility.
audiences.openingQuestion: When a physicist explains a phenomenon by a law, and that law by a deeper law, what makes the deepest one explanatory — and if it’s a brute fact, what is it passing up the chain?
audiences.avoid: Don’t frame God as a better physical hypothesis or pin the argument to the Big Bang. Don’t suggest science is unreliable; the argument is that science is *more* reliable than brute-fact naturalism can account for.

audiences.who: Philosophy student who knows the literature
audiences.startingPoint: Knows van Inwagen’s modal-collapse argument, the Hume–Edwards ‘explain the parts and you’ve explained the whole’ reply, and thinks PSR is a dubious rationalist dogma.
audiences.approach: Be precise about *which* PSR you defend. Present the Thomist construal: explanation as intelligibility, not entailment, and only concrete things and their attributes as explananda. Show how this defuses the big-conjunction argument. Lead with Della Rocca’s line-drawing dilemma and Feser’s extension (giving up all explicability arguments means giving up argument). Use the here-and-now route to sidestep composition worries. Distinguish strict from derivative necessity, and self-explanatory from self-caused.
audiences.openingQuestion: Which version of PSR are you rejecting — one that requires entailment and treats propositions as explananda, or one that only requires intelligibility of concrete beings? And where exactly do you draw Della Rocca’s line?
audiences.avoid: Don’t wave away the big-conjunction argument as ‘just a puzzle’ without giving the two-part reply. Don’t overstate: say the burden is on the critic to show PSR can be *coherently* denied, and don’t claim PSR is provable by direct demonstration.

audiences.who: Brute-fact atheist (‘the universe is just there, and that’s all’)
audiences.startingPoint: Explanations have to stop somewhere. Stopping at the universe is no worse, and more economical, than stopping at God.
audiences.approach: Agree that explanation must stop somewhere, then focus on the *kind* of stopping point: brute (explaining nothing) versus self-explanatory (able to ground everything else). Show that brute-fact stopping is either arbitrary (why only there?) or self-undermining (if brute facts are allowed, your beliefs could be brute too). Then show why the universe can’t be a self-explanatory stopping point: it changes, has parts, and is doubly contingent. Emphasize that God is not an unexplained stopping point; that is the asymmetry.
audiences.openingQuestion: Do you allow brute facts anywhere other than at the very bottom of reality? If not, what’s special about the bottom?
audiences.avoid: Don’t claim the brute-fact view is stupid; it is a serious position held by Russell and Mackie. Don’t slide into ‘everything has a cause,’ which hands them the ‘What caused God?’ reply.

audiences.who: Believer who knows popular apologetics (e.g., the kalam argument)
audiences.startingPoint: Thinks the argument is about the universe having a beginning, and uses ‘What caused God? — nothing, God is eternal’ as a quick answer.
audiences.approach: Show that this proof is *stronger* for granting an infinite past, and that its key question is dependence right now. Teach the difference between causes and reasons so they stop saying ‘everything that begins has a cause’ when they mean something else. Walk through Stage 2, since the step from ‘necessary being’ to God is where most amateur versions stop. Model honesty about what the argument does *not* show, such as the truth of any specific revelation.
audiences.openingQuestion: Would your argument still work if the universe turned out to be infinitely old? This one does — want to see why?
audiences.avoid: Avoid triumphalism and overclaiming. Don’t treat ‘necessary being’ as meaning ‘exists by definition’ (the ontological argument), and don’t skip the defense of PSR as if it were obvious to everyone.

audiences.startingPoint: Feels there is an ultimate reality but identifies it with the universe, nature, or ‘energy,’ and is wary of a personal God.
audiences.approach: Affirm the intuition that there is an ultimate, self-sufficient ground of things; the argument agrees. Then ask what such a ground must be like. It can’t change or have parts, because anything that does depends on something else. The universe and ‘energy’ change and have structure, so they depend on something deeper. Show how necessity leads to simplicity, unity, and intellect, and why the ultimate ground is distinct from the world while sustaining it at every moment.
audiences.openingQuestion: If there is something that everything else depends on, could it be something that itself changes and is made of parts?
audiences.avoid: Don’t dismiss their spiritual sense as confused. Don’t lead with doctrinal specifics. Keep it to what the argument shows: one, simple, necessary, intelligent cause of all.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I know the contingency argument: ‘everything needs an explanation, therefore God.’ But why should *everything* need an explanation? Maybe some things are just brute facts.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Fair question. When you find a puddle under your car, do you ever seriously consider that it’s there for no reason at all?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: No, but that’s because puddles have always had causes in my experience. That’s induction, not a law of reality.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Induction supports it, agreed. But try this. If things can happen for no reason, could your belief that some things happen for no reason have popped into your head for no reason?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: In principle, I suppose. But I believe it because of arguments.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Exactly — you assume the arguments are *why* you believe it, and that your mind tracks logic and truth. Those are claims about explanation. Once you allow things to happen for no reason, you lose the right to be confident of either, including about your case against the principle.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That feels like a trick. I can accept that *some* things lack explanations without thinking everything is random.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then where is the line? You accept explanatory reasoning in physics, in induction, in philosophy of mind. Why exempt the existence of things? ‘It’s just a brute fact that the line falls there’ assumes the very thing in dispute.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Say explanation stops at the fundamental laws of physics. Everything else is explained by them, and they just hold.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Picture a book resting on a shelf, and the shelf floating in midair for no reason at all. Is the book’s position explained?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Not really. But laws aren’t shelves.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The structure is the same. If the deepest law has nothing in it or beyond it that accounts for its holding, it has nothing to pass up the chain. The higher ‘explanations’ are borrowed from a lender who has no money.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: All right, suppose I grant the principle. The universe could be infinitely old, each state caused by the one before. Then everything is explained.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Leibniz asked you to imagine an infinite series of geometry books, each copied from an earlier one. Every copy has a cause, but why geometry? Why these laws, these kinds of things? And the series itself could have failed to exist.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That’s the fallacy of composition. Parts being contingent doesn’t make the whole contingent.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It depends on the property. Weight doesn’t transfer from parts to whole; color does — a wall of red bricks is red. Is a pile of three stones *less* dependent than one stone? It depends on each stone *and* on their arrangement. But I don’t even need the whole. Take your coffee mug. What explains its existing right now, this second?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Its atoms, and the forces holding them together.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Which are contingent too. So what keeps *them* in existence now? You get a chain of present dependencies. Finite or infinite, it’s all borrowed existence, and it needs something that exists by its own nature.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine: something necessary. Why not the universe itself, or the quantum field?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Ask what it takes to exist by your own nature. You can’t have potentials waiting to be actualized, or parts that must be held together, or existence you merely receive, because any of those makes you dependent. The universe changes and has parts, so it can’t be the necessary thing.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then what explains God? If you let God go unexplained, let the universe go unexplained.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: I don’t let God go unexplained. God’s existence is explained by his nature, which just is existence, pure actuality with nothing borrowed. The universe’s nature can’t do that. The contrast isn’t explained versus unexplained; it’s self-explanatory versus explained by another. And self-explanatory isn’t self-caused.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Van Inwagen’s objection, then. Take the conjunction of all contingent truths. If a necessary truth explains it, it’s entailed, so it’s necessary. Modal collapse.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That assumes explanation means entailment. Gravity explains elliptical orbits without entailing them, since other forces could interfere. The principle only asks that things be made intelligible. And propositions aren’t Platonic objects floating around needing their own explanation. Explain the concrete things and the minds that think about them, and nothing is left over.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Even if all this works, you’ve reached a necessary being, not the God of any religion.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: You’ve reached one, purely actual, simple, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, good cause of everything — the God of classical theism. Which religion, if any, has the fuller story is a further question. But if this works, atheism doesn’t.

socratic: When you can’t find the explanation for something, like where your keys went, do you conclude there isn’t one? Why not?
If things could happen for no reason at all, how could you be sure your present beliefs weren’t among them?
When an argument convinces you, do you think its being a good argument is *why* you believe the conclusion? What does that assume?
You accept explanations everywhere in science. What principle tells you to stop asking for explanations exactly at the existence of things?
If a shelf floated in midair for no reason, would it explain why the book on it doesn’t fall?
Is a pile of three stones more dependent, less dependent, or equally dependent compared with one stone?
If nothing in a tree’s nature guaranteed its existence when it first sprouted, does anything in its nature guarantee its existence right now?
Can making a chain of borrowers longer, even infinitely long, ever produce money that nobody borrowed?
What would something have to be like for its existence to follow from what it is?
Could something that changes, or that is made of parts, depend on nothing at all? What would it depend on?
Is ‘explained by its own nature’ the same as ‘caused itself’? What would causing yourself require?
Does the sun’s gravity *entail* that the planets move in ellipses, or does it make their motion intelligible? Which does an explanation need to do?

traps.trap: Saying ‘everything has a cause’ when you mean ‘everything has an explanation.’
traps.fix: Say ‘explanation’ or ‘sufficient reason’ from the start. Point out that causes are one kind of explanation, and that something can be explained by its own nature without being caused.

traps.trap: Leaning on the Big Bang or a first moment in time.
traps.fix: Grant an infinite past up front, as Feser does. Shift to dependence *now*: what keeps this thing in existence at this moment?

traps.trap: Treating PSR as self-evident and skipping its defense.
traps.fix: Give the reductio. Denying PSR undermines perception, reasoning, and scientific explanation. Then give Della Rocca’s line-drawing challenge.

traps.trap: Stopping at ‘there’s a necessary being’ and announcing ‘that’s God.’
traps.fix: Do Stage 2: necessity requires pure act, simplicity, and essence identical with existence. Then uniqueness, being the cause of all else, and the classical attributes. This is also what rules out the universe.

traps.trap: Getting bogged down in the big-conjunction argument before the listener understands the basic idea.
traps.fix: Hold it until asked. Then give the two-part reply briefly: explanation means intelligibility, not entailment; propositions aren’t free-floating objects needing explanation.

traps.trap: Framing the question as ‘why is there something rather than nothing?’
traps.fix: Ask instead ‘why are there any contingent things at all?’ The ‘nothing’ framing implies nothingness was possible, which the argument denies, and it invites detours into physics’ so-called nothing.

Explain metaphysical necessity: God cannot fail to exist because he has no potentials, parts, or received existence, not because of the meaning of a word. This keeps the ontological argument out of the discussion.

traps.trap: Overclaiming that the argument proves a particular religion.
traps.fix: State exactly what it concludes — one necessary, simple, purely actual, intelligent, good cause of all — and note that questions about revelation come later (ch7a).
